After dinner, she curls up on the couch with her family to watch a PG family film. In one scene, a character says something like, “Don’t lose your innocence,” and the adults chuckle in a way that makes the word sound like it means more than just “being nice.” She notices her mom quickly changes the subject when her brother asks what it means, and that makes the word stick in her mind.

Later, while her parents clean up and the movie keeps playing in the background, she takes the family tablet and opens an AI chat site she’s seen mentioned in comments and short videos. She types searches like “innocent love” and “what does innocence mean in romance” and watches how the system responds. She starts phrasing questions that feel like a test, trying to see if the AI will treat “innocence” as something people want in a boyfriend or girlfriend, or if it will act weird about it. She asks things like whether “innocent” is a compliment when someone likes you, why some stories say “innocent girls” are “more lovable,” and whether being “naive” makes a crush different—half because she’s genuinely confused by the movie line, and half because she wants to see where the boundary is and what the AI will say back.
